INTRODUCTIONM
As you learned in the previous two lessons, the AM Receiver Trainer consists of three (3) printed circuit cards.
The PC130-438 is the Microprocessor and Phase Lock Loop (PLL) that provides the synthesized tuning and channel display.
When manually tuned, the AM receiver need only consist of the PC130-439 and 440 circuit cards. All necessary components for AM Receiver operations are contained on these cards.....
Since most modern receivers employ synthesized tuning, the PC130-438 card should be used to facilitate the technician's understanding of PLL theory and operations.
Faults may occur in any of the components on the PC130-438 card. U2 contains the phase lock loop electronics. The microprocessor has a paper label affixed to it.
The block diagram below depicts the primary sections of the AM receiver. All faultable portions of the receiver are shown. The station detector, however, will NOT be faulted. 440 card.

SCHEMATIC ANALYSISE
DISCUSSION
Radio Frequency (RF) enters PC130-439 at the antenna input (TP1) which is actually an augmentation to the true antenna, L1.
L1 is a part of the tuner which is comprised of L1 and D1. D1 is a capacitive diode (a varactor) whose capacitance is varied by the amount of reverse voltage applied to it.
This voltage is determined by R9 when manually tuning the receiver..
During microprocessor operation, this voltage is provided by the PLL (U2, pin13) on PC130-438.
The receiver's overall frequency range is determined by R10. It should be adjusted to read 1.4 VDC at TP9.
D2 and L2 make up an oscillator that is "ganged" together with the tuner by voltage only.
The PLL issues a controlling voltage to D2 via Op Amp U2, which tunes the oscillator to the desired frequency. The desired frequency is 455kHz above the Tuned RF. kHz above the tuned RF.

The AM Front end converts the RF into IF. The received signal is boosted and returned to 455kHz higher than originally received. The new frequency signal is coupled through T1 and T2. T2 is tuned to a resonant frequency of 455kHz. The output of T2 is the signal intelligence at 455kHz plus sidebands (450 and 460 kHz).
The PLL receives feedback from T2 via Q2. received signal is only measurable in microvolts and is not of sufficient amplitude to be used, as is, by the receiver.

The newly converted IF is sent to the IF amplifier via a ceramic filter X1. X1 passes 455kHz only. U1 amplifies the IF and sends it to the detector. U1 gain is controlled by the automatic gain control (AGC) circuit.
Heterodyning is the process that allows us to convert one frequency to another without losing the intelligence. r without losing the intelligence.
The desired, resonant frequency is a modulated 455 kHz frequency that contains the intelligence from the original RF signal.
However, as a product of the heterodyning process, other frequencies are created.

There will be the two original frequencies as well as the sum and difference of those frequencies. The 455 kHz frequency, with its upper and lower sidebands, needs to be amplified. All other frequencies and harmonics are filtered out in the IF amplifier section.
The heterodyning process that creates the desired IF also produces several unwanted frequencies. X1, U1, and T3 rid the receiver of all but 455kHz and sidebands.
The cleaned and amplified IF signal can be measured at TP7, which is the IF output to PC130-440.

As mentioned, the 455 kHz IF signal contains the intelligence from the original tuned RF signal. In order for the intelligence to be usable, it must first be extracted from the 455 kHz IF. The AM Detector circuitry performs this job using the diode D1.

D1 conducts only during the positive portion of the incoming IF signal. This removes the bottom half of the waveform. The filters that follow it remove the remaining modulation and frequencies as illustrated below.
The capacitor C3 blocks the DC level that the detected signal rides on, leaving only the original intelligence to be amplified in the AF amplifier section.
The detected audio signal is fed to the Station Detector, the Automatic Gain Control (AGC) and the Audio Amplifier.
The Station Detector is controlled by the incoming signal and the variable resistor, R4. R4 is the threshold control that sets the voltage to the non-inverting (+) input of the comparator U2.
When the inverting input (-) at pin 2 is more positive than the
non-inverting input (+) at pin 3, the output goes low, properly biasing DS1, causing it to illuminate.
The Automatic Gain Control (AGC) provides a stable output signal level from the IF amplifier circuit regardless of variations in the RF input.
The variable resistor R8 is the AGC adjust that provides voltage to the inverting input (-) pin 2, U3. Pin 3 of U3 is the non-inverting input for the detected AM signal.

The output of U3 is at pin 6 and can be measured at TP5. This voltage feeds back to PC130-439 at pin 5, U3, the IF amplifier. Any variation in the incoming RF signal causes U3 on PC130-440 to increase or decrease its output voltage.

As mentioned previously, the detected audio signal also goes to the Audio Amplifier stage. While headsets could be used to listen to the signal without an audio amplifier, practicality suggests using a conventional speaker. Hence, the amplifier.
The audio signal enters the AF amplifier (U1) at pin 3. The signal is then amplified and routed to the output at pin 5. Once amplified, the signal is of adequate amplitude to drive the speaker.
The Phase Lock Loop theory has already been discussed in the previous lesson. One important fact to remember is that PLL circuitry is only active when the microprocessor is employed. .
With the tuning select switch on PC130-439 in the manual position, the PLL, microprocessor and related components are effectively removed from the receiver. A pinout of the PLL (U2) is shown below.

Much of the phase-lock loop components shown in the block diagram are contained in the IC chip, U2 on the PC130-438 card. U2 is a nearly self-contained PLL that is directly governed by the microprocessor. y their VCO which is U2 on the PC130-439 card.

2. The VCO's output is always 455 kHz higher than the incoming tuned RF.
3. The received RF signal must be amplified because it is too small to be usable by the receiver.
4. T1 and X1 are the primary resonant filters that allow only the 455 kHz frequency and the sidebands at 450 kHz and 460 kHz to pass into the IF amp, U3.
5. In the AM Receiver, the detected intelligence is in the USB only. All other portions of the AM envelope are rejected.
6. AGC provides a stable output despite fluctuations in the tuned RF.
7. The AF amplifier is necessary to boost the audio signal to levels high enough to drive a speaker.

The incoming RF and the VCO signal meet at transformer T1. The resulting frequency is 455 kHz, which is connected to transformer T2. The center tap of T2 develops the PLL feedback signal. Both transformers are tunable for optimum frequency performance for the 455 kHz center frequency and sidebands.

Providing good selectivity in the IF amplifier stage of an AM receiver is a major goal of the designer and is the prime reason that resonant filters are used.
Ideally, these filters would pass all frequencies between 450 kHz and 460 kHz while rejecting all others. Notice the difference between the ideal response and the typical response.
The sides of the response curve are called "skirts" and the steeper the skirts the better the filter.
The bandwidth of a filter is determined by the distance in Hertz between the two half power points. A half power point is the frequency at which Eout = 0.707 x Eout maximum.

The half power points are located on either side of the center frequency. In the case of IF filters, the bandwidth should be at least 10 kHz. e output voltage at the 450 kHz and 460 kHz frequencies should not be less than 70% of the output voltage at 455 kHz.

The gain of the IF amplifier(s) in a receiver determines the unit's sensitivity (the ability to detect and lock on to a weak signal).

Some understanding of the amount of gain in a typical IF section is necessary for effective troubleshooting. The ability to work with gain in terms of either voltage ratio or dB level is a prerequisite to the study of radio communications.

Normally, the gain of an amplifier is the ratio of AC collector voltage to AC base voltage. In the case of transformer coupled stages, as in IF amplifiers, gain is calculated as the ratio of AC secondary voltage to AC primary voltage, or the base of one stage to the base of the next stage.
The gain of amplifier stages may be expressed either as a voltage ratio or as a decibel level, where: Gain dB = 20 LOG (Eo/Ein).

While no AGC circuit is capable of maintaining a perfectly constant output, many of the more advanced designs offer quite respectable performance.
There are two basic categories of AGC circuits; carrier derived (also known as IF derived) and audio derived.
In carrier derived AGC, the AGC voltage is produced by rectifying and filtering the signal carrier in the IF section. on.
In audio derived AGC, the AGC voltage is produced by rectifying and filtering the audio signal voltage.

The next portion of the experiment will allow you to observe the actions of the AM Detector circuitry.
The purpose of the AM Detector circuit is to recover the original intelligence from the modulated carrier frequency.
The intelligence is carried in the upper and lower sidebands of the 455 kHz carrier which comprise the top and bottom boundaries of the AM envelope.

A low pass filter following the detector diode removes all of the IF signal except the USB. This is due to the fact that the diode is only conducting when the positive portion of the envelope is felt.

Simple AM detectors do not perform well under all conditions. At high modulation levels and/or high audio frequencies, distortion of the recovered audio begins to develop due to the time constant of the low-pass filter.
At low modulation levels, distortion is created by the detector diode because a finite voltage is required to forward bias the diode. o
In lieu of this, detector diodes are always germanium because only 0.2 volts are required to forward bias the P-N junction, rather than 0.7 in silicon diodes.

AGC circuitry is used to maintain a constant output signal regardless of variations in the input signal.

Carrier derived AGC is far more common than audio derived AGC. In any AGC circuit it is important that no AC signal be present on the AGC line. Any AC, especially audio, represents a form of AC feedback and may cause oscillations.
